Metrics, Analytics & Experimentation  ·  Experimentation & Causal Inference

When You Can't A/B Test

When randomisation is off the table, what is the honest alternative — and how do you know it is honest?

1A city that will not hold still

On the first Monday of September 2026, Rohan Deshmukh, VP of Product at Shravan Mobility, opened a spreadsheet he had been avoiding for a week. Shravan ran a ride-and-parcel marketplace across Pune and Nagpur — about 9,000 active drivers, 40,000 parcel deliveries a day, and a dispatch engine that matched riders to drivers in real time. His team had built something they called smart batching: instead of sending one driver on one parcel run, the algorithm would look for two or three deliveries heading roughly the same way and pool them onto a single trip. In simulation, batching cut the cost per delivery by close to ten percent. If that number held in the real world, it was worth roughly ₹40 lakh a month in the two cities combined, and the board wanted a recommendation before the November 1 review.

Rohan's instinct, honed on years of running feature experiments, was to do what Shravan always did: randomise half the users into batching, hold the other half back as control, and read the result off a dashboard in three weeks. He drafted the ticket. Then his data scientist, Priya Iyer, stopped by his desk with a question that unravelled the plan. "Which half of the drivers," she asked, "are you going to randomise?" Batching did not just change what happened to a treated delivery — it changed which driver was available for the next delivery, treated or not. A driver serving a batched route was off the road longer per trip but handling more parcels; that changed queue lengths and wait times for everyone nearby, including riders and drivers in the "control" group. Pune's driver-rider marketplace was one interconnected system, not 9,000 independent little experiments. Randomising by user would not isolate the effect of batching — it would smear it across both arms of the test and hand Rohan a number he could not trust either way. He had six weeks and a board date, and the textbook tool he reached for first did not apply.

Figure 1. In a marketplace, a driver's assignment to "batching" changes availability for every nearby driver and rider — including the ones assigned to "control." The two arms are not statistically independent, which is the condition an A/B test quietly assumes.

2The idea

An A/B test — a randomised controlled experiment in which independent units are assigned by chance to a treatment or control condition so that the only systematic difference between the groups is the treatment itself — rests on an assumption statisticians call SUTVA, the stable unit treatment value assumption: one unit's assigned condition must not affect another unit's outcome. When it does, the label "control" stops meaning "unaffected." "When you can't A/B test" is the name for the working set of alternative designs — before/after comparisons instrumented with guardrail metrics, switchback tests, geographic or account-level holdouts, and structured qualitative tests — that product and growth teams reach for when SUTVA breaks, when there are too few independent units to reach statistical power, or when practical and ethical constraints rule randomisation out entirely.

The idea was not invented so much as inherited and adapted. Ronald Fisher formalised randomised experimental design in agricultural field trials in the 1920s, and for decades the unit of randomisation — a plot of land, then a patient, then a website visitor — was assumed to be independent of its neighbours by construction. Digital marketplaces broke that assumption in the 2010s: economists including Susan Athey and experimentation teams inside companies like Lyft, Uber and DoorDash published on "interference" and popularised the switchback test — randomising time windows rather than individual users — as the practical fix for two-sided markets. The sentence Rohan could say in the boardroom without sounding glib: "When treatment and control can bleed into each other, the question isn't whether to randomise — it's what to randomise, and if the honest answer is nothing at the user level, we build a guardrail-based design instead of pretending we ran a clean test."

3How it actually works

The first step, and the one practitioners most often skip, is diagnosis: naming precisely why a standard user-level A/B test will not work here, because the diagnosis determines which alternative is honest. Shravan's problem was interference through a shared physical system — drivers on the same roads, the same rider queue. A B2B software company with eighteen enterprise accounts has a different problem: too few independent units to ever reach statistical power, no matter how cleanly you randomise. A company changing prices for walk-in retail customers has a third problem: no practical way to show two customers standing at the same counter two different prices. Each diagnosis points to a different fix, and conflating them is the single most common error in this area.

Once the failure mode is named, the second step is choosing the design that neutralises it rather than one that merely feels rigorous. If interference travels through time-bound shared infrastructure — a city's roads, a factory's line — a switchback test randomises whole time blocks to treatment or control, so that during any given block everyone experiences the same condition and spillover has nowhere to leak. If the population is simply too small to power a user-level test, a before/after design with guardrails becomes the least-bad option: measure the metric before and after launch against a baseline that controls for seasonality — the same period a year earlier, or a synthetic control built by weighting comparable markets that did not get the change — while tracking guardrail metrics that would move if something other than the treatment were driving the result. If the units are physical locations, a geographic or store-level holdout preserves the interference boundary by matching pilot markets to statistically similar control markets. If none of the above yields a trustworthy number, a qualitative test — structured interviews, a concierge or "wizard of oz" trial, a small diary study — trades a quantified estimate for a directional, causally-informed judgment, still more honest than a fabricated point estimate.

The third step, almost always skipped under deadline pressure, is writing the decision rule before the data arrives: the exact combination of primary-metric movement and guardrail behaviour that will trigger rollback, hold, or scale-up. Without it, ambiguous results get argued into whatever conclusion the room already wanted.

4A worked example

Priya proposed a switchback test. She divided Pune's operating day into 2-hour blocks and ran the test for 21 days, giving 252 blocks in total. Each block was randomly assigned to "batching on" or "batching off," stratified by day of week and by peak versus off-peak hour so the two arms would not accidentally differ in mix — 126 blocks each. The metric was average cost per delivery within a block.

ConditionMean cost/deliveryStd. deviationBlocks (n)
Batching ON₹42.30₹9.80126
Batching OFF₹47.10₹10.20126

The raw difference was ₹4.80 per delivery, a 10.2% reduction — close to the simulation's promise. To know whether that gap was signal or noise, Priya computed the standard error of the difference: SE = √((9.80²/126) + (10.20²/126)) = √(0.762 + 0.826) = √1.588 ≈ ₹1.26. The t-statistic was 4.80 ÷ 1.26 ≈ 3.81, comfortably past the 1.96 threshold for 95% confidence, giving a confidence interval of ₹4.80 ± (1.96 × 1.26) = ₹4.80 ± ₹2.47, or roughly ₹2.33 to ₹7.27 saved per delivery. That range, not the single ₹4.80 figure, was what Rohan took to the board: batching plausibly saved somewhere between ₹2.33 and ₹7.27 per delivery, with 95% confidence, in the design as run.

Priya then re-ran the arithmetic changing one input: what if the blocks were 30 minutes instead of two hours, to "get more data points" faster? Nominal sample size jumps to roughly 2,016 blocks across the same three weeks — an apparent embarrassment of riches. But a driver mid-way through a batched route when a block flips to "off" keeps behaving like a batching-affected driver for several more minutes: adjacent short blocks are no longer independent observations, they are autocorrelated slices of the same underlying process. Correcting for that serial correlation with a block bootstrap, Priya's effective sample size fell to roughly 300 independent blocks, and the standard error roughly doubled to about ₹2.50, dragging the t-statistic down to about 1.9 — barely at the edge of significance for the very same underlying effect.

Block lengthNominal nEffective n (autocorrelation-adjusted)SE of differencet-statistic
2 hours252≈252₹1.263.81
30 minutes2,016≈300≈₹2.50≈1.90

Nothing about batching's true effect had changed between the two rows. What changed was the block length, and with it the number of genuinely independent observations the design produced. The lesson Rohan wrote at the top of his notes: in a switchback test, block length is not a tuning knob for "more data" — it is the boundary that determines whether you are measuring 252 independent facts or 300 independent facts dressed up as 2,016.

5The nuances a learner must sit with

Interference is not the same as "we have no counterfactual"

Some teams reach for a before/after design because they believe they have no counterfactual at all. That is rarely true. The counterfactual usually exists — a comparable time period, a comparable market — but it is contaminated by the treatment leaking into it. Naming which of the two problems you actually have changes which fix is honest.

A switchback test is not a magic exemption from statistics

It still needs enough independent time blocks to power a real comparison, and it is sensitive to carryover at block boundaries, as the worked example showed. Teams that treat it as a free pass to skip power calculations end up with false confidence dressed as rigour.

Before/after with guardrails is the weakest of the honest options

It is vulnerable to seasonality, competitor moves, and macro trends unrelated to the treatment. It earns trust only when paired with guardrail metrics the treatment plausibly could not move, and when the effect size is large relative to normal period-to-period noise.

Geo and account holdouts require real matching, not geography as a proxy

Picking "Pune as treatment, Nagpur as control" only works if the two cities are statistically comparable on order volume, driver density and seasonality, established through matching or historical correlation — not because they happen to be nearby cities the team already operates in.

Qualitative tests answer "why" and "whether," not "how much"

A dozen well-run interviews can tell Rohan with real confidence that riders notice longer batched waits and dislike them. They cannot tell him whether that dislike will cost 2% or 20% of retention, and attaching a fabricated percentage to a qualitative finding is a bigger sin than presenting no number at all.

"We didn't have time to A/B test" is not "we cannot A/B test"

The former is a resourcing failure dressed in the vocabulary of the latter. A genuine SUTVA violation or a genuinely small population justifies an alternative design; a missed sprint deadline does not, and the two get conflated constantly.

None of these designs explain the mechanism, even when they nail the number

A switchback test can tell Rohan that batching saves ₹4.80 per delivery with tight confidence and still leave him unable to say whether the saving comes from fewer empty miles or fewer idle drivers — which is why driver interviews and ride-along observation remain part of a serious answer, not a decoration on top of it.

Peeking is more dangerous here, not less

Interference-based designs already produce noisier estimates than a clean A/B test. The temptation to check daily and stop the moment it looks good is stronger, and the damage larger — which is why the pre-registered decision rule from Section 3 is the whole safeguard, not an optional extra.

6Consumer, B2B, marketplace — and early-stage versus scale

The shape of the problem changes with the shape of the business. In a two-sided marketplace like Shravan Mobility, interference is spatial and temporal — shared roads, shared driver pools, shared queues — so switchback tests are usually right, because the unit needing randomisation is a slice of shared time, not a person. In a B2B company with a handful of large accounts — picture Kartik FinServ, an enterprise lending-software vendor with eighteen bank clients — the problem is rarely interference; eighteen is simply nowhere near enough independent units to power any test. There, before/after with tightly matched accounts, phased rollouts using the next cohort as an informal comparison, and structured account-manager interviews carry more evidential weight than any p-value could. Early-stage consumer products share that problem for a different reason: not too few possible units in principle, but too few actual users yet, so qualitative and concierge-style tests dominate regardless of design sophistication. At larger scale, particularly in physical retail — a national grocery chain like Vaishakh Foods redesigning shelf layouts across hundreds of stores — the interference problem returns in a different guise, solved by test markets: a handful of matched pilot stores compared against matched control stores, the store-level analogue of a geo holdout, and exactly the design this topic unlocks for retail.

7Common mistakes

The unguarded before/after. Symptom: a team ships a change, sees a metric jump the following week, and declares victory with no comparison to anything else. Underlying misunderstanding: mistaking a time-trend for a treatment effect. Cheapest diagnostic: check a metric the change could not plausibly have moved — if that guardrail metric jumped by a similar margin at the same time, the "win" is a seasonal or macro artefact, not the treatment.

Switchback blocks too short to be independent. Symptom: an enormous nominal sample size and a suspiciously tight confidence interval. Underlying misunderstanding: treating adjacent time blocks as statistically independent when carryover links them. Cheapest diagnostic: plot the metric's autocorrelation across consecutive blocks, or simply compare the first and last five minutes of each block — if they differ systematically, the block boundary is leaking.

Quantifying a qualitative finding. Symptom: "we talked to twelve users and they loved it, so we're projecting an 8% lift." Underlying misunderstanding: borrowing the confident vocabulary of a quantitative test for a design that was never built to produce a point estimate. Cheapest diagnostic: ask when the 8% figure was decided — if it postdates the interviews rather than a pre-registered threshold, it is a narrative dressed as data.

The n-of-two holdout. Symptom: a B2B team excludes two accounts from a rollout, watches them underperform the rest, and calls it proof. Underlying misunderstanding: forgetting that with only two control units, ordinary noise can explain almost any outcome. Cheapest diagnostic: ask how many different reasonable choices of "which two accounts to hold out" would have flipped the conclusion — if the answer is "several," the result was never robust.

8What good looks like

At Vaishakh Foods, Ananya Kulkarni faced a structurally similar problem the same quarter: a new electronic shelf-tagging system, too expensive to roll out to all 340 stores blind. She picked eight pilot stores matched on footfall, basket size and regional mix against eight statistically similar control stores; pre-registered a decision rule — roll out chain-wide only if sales lift exceeded 3% while stockout rate and staff hours per shift moved by no more than 5% in the wrong direction; ran the comparison for ten weeks, the length her team had calculated was needed to detect a 3% lift given normal store-to-store variance; and paired the quantitative result with in-store interviews that explained why the lift was concentrated in the produce section and not in packaged goods. The board got a number with an honest confidence interval and a mechanism, not a hunch dressed as certainty. Rohan later adopted the same discipline for Shravan's next dispatch change, before the interference problem even had a chance to surprise him twice.

9Closing

Rohan recommended a phased city-wide rollout of smart batching, gated on the switchback-confirmed range of ₹2.33–₹7.27 saved per delivery, with driver-earnings variance and cancellation rate written in as guardrails and a 90-day recheck once volumes were higher. He did not present the ₹4.80 point estimate alone, and he did not let the board treat the switchback test as equivalent in certainty to a clean user-level A/B test — he said so explicitly, and asked for a wider buffer in the rollout budget because of it. The reasoning he gave was the one Priya had taught him in September: the honest question was never "did we run an experiment," it was "did we correctly identify what could not be randomised, and choose a design that respected that limit instead of pretending it did not exist."

From here, the natural next topics are quasi-experiments and causal inference more broadly — difference-in-differences and synthetic control methods that formalise the "matched comparison" intuition Ananya used at Vaishakh Foods — and, separately, the discipline of running test markets in physical retail and experimentation with few, large customers, both of which generalise the small-n and matching problems this topic only sketched. Two questions worth sitting with: when your team says "we can't A/B test this," are they naming a real SUTVA violation or population limit, or a deadline they would rather not admit to? And when you last trusted a before/after number, what guardrail metric would have told you, honestly, if you were wrong?
case40v1-exp.when:
Doraha Systems: The Sequence Nobody Could Randomise

Pune · Sunday, 15 November 2026

1. The night before

At twenty past eleven on Sunday night, Lalini Thiara had two laptops open at her dining table off Baner Road. One held the board pre-read she had signed off four days earlier, whose page six carried one bold sentence: Sequence 7 cut roll-forward into Bucket 2 by 30 per cent at our largest NBFC client. The other held a four-page note in from Lehmber Thethi in Toronto on Friday, which never used the number thirty.

By nine next morning she had to tell Loveleen Tangri in Bengaluru whether to file seven content templates with the telecom registry, the only route to four more lenders on 1 December, and Luvraj Tehlan in Jersey City whether the thirty per cent could stay in a deck going out on 24 November. On 10 December she faced the board.

What she had never had was a randomised test.

2. How Doraha got here

Doraha Systems Private Limited was founded in Pune in March 2017 to do one narrow thing: decide which borrower gets which reminder, in what order and channel, before and after an instalment falls due. It sequences messages, voice calls, UPI AutoPay attempts and field-visit allocations in the early buckets. By FY26 it carried 72.5 lakh accounts across twelve tenants on ₹48.6 crore (Exhibit 1). Thiara co-founded it and runs product.

A constraining decision came in July 2021. To win its first large non-banking financial company, Doraha accepted a clause its own founders read as boilerplate: no borrower of the Client shall receive a materially different communication sequence from another borrower in the same delinquency bucket and product class, save with the Client's prior written consent. It now sits in nine of twelve master agreements, all five NBFC ones among them. It shaped the code too: the configuration store was keyed on tenant, product class and bucket, and nothing else. There has never been a second slot to put a control group in.

3. The industry

Two-wheeler and consumer-durable lending in India is dominated by NBFCs and the manufacturers' captive arms; the collections software round it is sold by Credgenics, Spocto and Lentra against in-house builds. Doraha sells conduct, not coverage: a sequence that recovers money without generating complaints.

Conduct is where the regulation lives. The Reserve Bank's 2022 circular on recovery agents confines borrower contact to 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.; its Digital Lending Guidelines make the lender answerable for its service provider; TRAI requires every header and template registered and scrubbed for do-not-disturb; and NPCI fixes a pre-debit notification a day before a scheduled AutoPay debit, so one of Sequence 7's five touches is not Doraha's. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 binds Doraha to its tenants' stated purposes, and whether the product works is not among them.

The twelfth tenant is Dukkan Retail Group LLC of Dubai, selling electronics on instalments through 61 stores in the UAE and Oman. It pays ₹282.61 per account a year against ₹50.23 from the NBFC book, and its contract forbids exporting UAE events (Figure 2).

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In February 2026 Labhya Tandan flew from Berlin to Nagpur and Jalandhar and sat with nineteen borrowers. Nine could not say, unprompted, what day their EMI was due. Her recommendation was a pre-due sequence: tell people before, not after. It was believed testable.

In April, Doraha proposed a borrower-level A/B test on Daulat Finserv Limited's two-wheeler book — 3.85 lakh of its 9.6 lakh accounts on the platform, all falling due on the fifth. Thiara's team read the 2021 clause as admitting a pilot; Daulat's legal head read it as barring one without written consent, which goes to a credit committee that sits quarterly, next on 12 January 2027. That reading has not been revisited. In May, Tangri scoped a second sequence slot at two weeks; on 12 August she re-estimated it at six, most of that the allocator, which ranks a hub's queue as a whole.

Doraha fell back on a before-and-after with guardrails, and the baseline opened on 1 June. Sub-codes for pre-due message and autopay retry reached the ticketing picklist on 28 August, four days before Sequence 7 went live. Sequence 7 went live on Tuesday 1 September 2026 — carrying two changes, not one: the pre-due message and the new AutoPay retry schedule shipped together, the retry change already in the release train and Lakhveer Tagra unwilling to hold it a week. Thiara approved that in a two-line reply recorded nowhere. The second pre-due message cleared template registration only on 18 September, after that month's due date, so September is partially treated and October the only fully treated month (Figure 1, Exhibit 2).

On 7 October, Lochana Thappa circulated a note saying the guardrail breach (Exhibit 5) came from field-visit complaints, not messages. Through 21 September, 94 of 402 complaints carried a pre-due sub-code, 23.4 per cent. Over September it was 318 of 702, in October 362 of 768 — 45.3 and 47.1 per cent. Nobody re-sent it.

5. The people

Loveleen Tangri, director of engineering, Bengaluru. A second sequence slot is six weeks and she will not promise it faster twice. Four of her six engineers are locked until 20 December on a DPDP consent-ledger rebuild. Not saying: four of those weeks are the allocator, which she wants rewritten.

Lakhveer Tagra, staff platform engineer, Pune. A weekly switchback is the only design the scheduler can serve, and he wrote it. Not saying: the switch reuses a cron path that silently skipped two Sundays in July.

Labhya Tandan, principal designer, Berlin. The forty interviews (Exhibit 6) should finish before anything is extended; the sequence is her design and the complaints data the only threat to it. Not saying: twenty-six are unscheduled and she has no Marathi moderator after 30 November.

Lehmber Thethi, lead data scientist, Toronto. The thirty per cent compares two single months' counts. He has wanted a holdout since April. Not saying: his seasonal correction rests on two prior years and carries no interval.

Lochana Thappa, director of customer success, Singapore. Daulat is delighted, the renewal is on 30 November, and nothing should be reopened first. Renewals are 60 per cent of her variable pay. Not saying: Daulat's collections head told her he had stopped reading the complaints dashboard in September, which is in no note.

Luvraj Tehlan, head of sales for North America, Jersey City. The thirty per cent is what makes Doraha legible to a US buyer, and 4.2 standard errors more rigour than any competitor shows. His 24 November prospect is his largest. Not saying: he has said the number out loud on two calls.

Lavanjali Tuggal, head of collections operations, Dukkan Retail Group, Dubai. Wants Sequence 7 from January and will randomise borrowers if asked, her contract having no uniformity clause. Her bonus turns on 90-day recovery. Not saying: she is also in procurement talks with a competitor.

6. Exhibits

7. Voices

Product review, Pune, Thursday 12 November, 18:30 IST

Tehlan: “12,500 accounts rolling in August, 8,750 in October. That is thirty per cent. Their own file.”

Thethi: “Both are right. The inflow also fell, 43,100 to 38,900, and it falls every year. On rates it is 29.0 to 22.5 — a 22.4 per cent fall, not thirty.”

Tehlan: “Four point two standard errors, Lehmber. Your number.”

Thethi: “Mine. The standard error is about the counting. It says nothing about whether 2025 is the right 2025.”

Email, Tuggal to Thiara, Sunday 15 November, 14:20 GST

“Lalini — Ramadan instalment season starts in February and I want Sequence 7 before it. My legal has no uniformity clause, so split my book any way you like. I would rather be where you learn it than where you ship it.”

Engineering channel, Friday 13 November, evening IST

Tagra: “1 September shipped the pre-due message and the new retry schedule together. September had one message of two and the full retry change: 76.0. October had both: 77.5.”

Tangri: “So the retry change may be the whole thing, and we have no month where it ran alone.”

Tandan: “Nine of my nineteen in February could not name their due date. Five of the fourteen since were reading Hindi in a Marathi district.”

Thappa: “Daulat's field cost is down 3,400 visits a month at ₹240. Annualise that month-pair and it is ₹97.92 lakh against a fee of ₹4.8 crore. Nobody there asks me about cure rates.”

8. The options as Thiara sees them

She had written them out on Saturday.

A. Extend on the Daulat evidence. File the seven templates on Monday, take Sequence 7 to the four remaining NBFC tenants on 1 December, keep the 41.0 guardrail. Costs ₹18 lakh. Leaves the 2021 clause, the single-slot configuration store and Dukkan as they are.

B. Switchback on Daulat. Alternate Sequence 6 and Sequence 7 by calendar week across the whole two-wheeler book for twelve weeks from 1 December; every borrower in a bucket gets the same sequence in a given week. Costs ₹26 lakh, four engineers for six weeks, Daulat's written consent, and a freeze on other changes to that book until 1 March.

C. Holdout at Dirba. Keep 8 per cent of Dirba's 3.1 lakh personal-loan accounts on Sequence 6 indefinitely. Costs ₹14 lakh for the second slot, Dirba's board consent, and the fifteen-day borrower notice its counsel wants for a new processing purpose. Reads out on personal loans, average ticket ₹38,000; leaves the Daulat renewal untouched.

D. Stagger across Daulat's hubs. Sequence 7 to 52 Vidarbha hubs on 1 December, 49 Marathwada hubs on 1 January, 47 Madhya Pradesh and Chhattisgarh hubs on 1 February. Costs ₹9 lakh beyond the second slot, and Daulat's written consent to run two sequences in one product class for ninety days. Moves the rollout to February.

E. Finish the field work. Complete the remaining twenty-six interviews and eight ride-alongs, add a payment-diary study, extend nothing before 15 January. Costs ₹11 lakh and a Marathi moderator Doraha has not hired. Signs the renewal without the October number; Sequence 7 stays live on Daulat.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

Money. The FY27 product-engineering budget is ₹2.4 crore, of which ₹1.76 crore is committed, leaving ₹64 lakh. The five options as costed sum to ₹78 lakh.

People. Four of Tangri's six Bengaluru engineers are on the DPDP consent-ledger rebuild until 20 December, and that date is not hers to move. Tagra is one person.

Regulation. Template registration takes seven working days, so a Monday filing clears on Wednesday 25 November. Borrower contact is confined to 08:00–19:00. The NPCI pre-debit notification is fixed a day ahead of the debit. A new processing purpose needs the tenant's written instruction.

Contracts. The uniformity clause binds nine of twelve tenants and all five NBFCs. Daulat's agreement renews on Monday 30 November and its change freeze runs 1 December to 15 January. Dukkan's annexe keeps UAE events out of Pune.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Exhibit 2 gives October's cure rate as 77.5 per cent in one column and 86.2 in another. Which denominator belongs in a board paper, and what does that do to page six?
  2. Exhibit 3 sets a +5.2-point seasonal lift against the +6.4 observed in 2026. What must be true of 2024 and 2025 for that subtraction to identify Sequence 7's effect?
  3. Exhibit 4 puts the borrower-level minimum detectable effect at 1.3 points. What stands between that figure and a randomised test here, and which of it can a product leader move?
  4. The guardrail was 41.0 complaints per lakh nudges and was exceeded in both pilot months. Who could have stopped the pilot, on what information, and by when? What must a guardrail be made of to work here?
  5. Sequence 7 changed two things at once. Design the cheapest study Doraha could begin on 16 November that would move a reasonable person by 10 December; state its decision rule first, and what it cannot tell you.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Thiara do, in what order — and on 10 December, what does she say to a board that has read page six?

Sunday, 23:50

The flat had gone cold. Thiara put Thethi's note beside the pre-read and read the first paragraph of each again, and then a third time. Tuggal's message sat unanswered, eight hours old. Toronto was early afternoon and Thethi was online, the green dot steady beside his name. She typed can we talk, looked at it, and deleted it.

She opened the template filing form instead. Seven rows, each wanting a sequence ID in the first field, and the form would not let her leave it blank. Outside, a truck went down Baner Road and the windows shook, and then it was quiet.
case20v1-exp.when:
Chaman Basket: Fees Before Diwali

A teaching case on measuring a change when customers cannot be randomly split

1. Opening

Monday 19 October 2026, 8.40 a.m. Kamaljit Sahni, head of product at Chaman Basket, sat in a glass-walled room in HSR Layout, Bengaluru, with a one-page memo from the chief executive. By Friday 23 October she had to say how the company's new delivery-fee schedule would go live, and how anyone would know afterwards whether it had worked.

The schedule itself was simple. The flat ₹25 delivery fee would give way to ₹35 between 6 and 10 pm and ₹15 at every other hour, to ease an evening crush that was wearing out riders. The calendar was less simple. Diwali falls on Sunday 8 November, and city operations wanted the schedule live on Monday 26 October, before the festive peak. Chaman Basket's experiments normally split customers at random, and Kamaljit already suspected that would not work here. Her question was narrower than the chief executive's: not whether to launch, but which comparison she could defend to the board when results arrived on 16 November.

2. Company background

Chaman Basket sells groceries, fresh produce, dairy and festive sweets for delivery in about fifteen minutes from 38 dark stores: 16 in Bengaluru, 12 in Hyderabad and 10 in Pune. Founded in 2021 by two former supply-chain managers from Ludhiana, it has raised ₹310 crore across three rounds and handles about 15,000 orders a day at an average basket of ₹480. Roughly four in five orders are paid by UPI, with Razorpay as the gateway.

The competition is close and well funded. Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart serve the same neighbourhoods, BigBasket under the Tata group offers its own quick delivery, and Flipkart Minutes has appeared in the larger cities. Chaman Basket competes on fresh produce, Amul dairy and a festive range from local sweet makers.

Riders are gig partners paid per delivery, with evening incentives that cost more every festive season. Engineering sits in Bengaluru and Pune, design in Berlin, data science in Toronto and customer success in Singapore, so any Friday decision is also a negotiation between time zones.

3. The situation

Evenings were the problem. In Diwali week last year only 79 per cent of orders reached customers within fifteen minutes, against 88 per cent in the week of 29 September (Exhibit 2). Riders cancelled shifts, queues grew at the dark stores, and the company paid larger incentives to coax riders back. The proposed schedule (Exhibit 1) would be revenue-neutral if half of all orders still fell in the 6 to 10 pm band, since half at ₹35 and half at ₹15 average ₹25. The hope was that some customers would order earlier.

The product team's usual tool, a random split of customers, sat badly with that hope. Keerat Sidhu, the data scientist in Toronto, pointed out that two neighbours in one Hyderabad housing society would see ₹25 and ₹35 at 8 pm, and that both would draw on the same riders and the same shelves, so each group's experience depended on the other's. Splitting by store left 19 stores per side, and because weekly orders differ between stores by about 30 per cent, only a swing larger than roughly 27 per cent would show. The team hoped for 3 to 5 per cent.

Engineers in Pune reported that a store-level fee flag already existed, used for local promotions, and that rotating it by day would take about four days to build. A customer-level flag would take none. The Central Consumer Protection Authority's 2023 guidelines on dark patterns required every fee to be shown in full before payment, which the app already did.

The decision call was fixed for 7.30 pm IST on Friday 23 October, which is 4.00 pm in Berlin and 10.00 am in Toronto. Figure 1 shows how little room the calendar left.

4. The people

Kartar Slathia, head of city operations, Hyderabad. He runs the dark stores and rider pools. He wants the schedule live everywhere on 26 October. Every week of 79 per cent on-time delivery, he says, costs him riders he cannot replace before Diwali. He also knows that eleven of the 38 stores (four in Bengaluru, four in Hyderabad, three in Pune) sit far enough from their neighbours to have rider pools of their own.

Keerat Sidhu, data scientist, Toronto. She wants a comparison group and a written decision rule before launch. She has tested a method that compares a handful of stores with the rest: pretending to launch at six stores on 14 September, her predicted weekly orders came within 1.1 to 3.4 per cent of actual.

Kashish Sehgal, senior designer, Berlin. She wants no customer to feel singled out. In Germany, she says, a price that differed between two doors on one street would become a news story; Indian customers are more used to dynamic fees, but a housing-society WhatsApp group is a fast route to a screenshot. Last week she interviewed nine regular evening customers (five in Bengaluru, four in Hyderabad): six said they would order earlier to avoid ₹35, and three said they would simply pay it.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 sets out the fees, Exhibit 2 last year's festive weeks and Exhibit 3 the options described in section 6.

6. The options

Option A: launch everywhere and compare with the past. All 38 stores move to the new schedule on Monday 26 October. The company compares 26 October to 15 November with the three weeks before, using last year's festive pattern as a guide.

Option B: a switchback. Each store's days are randomly assigned to the new or old schedule, balanced by weekday, with the fee fixed from 5 am to 5 am the next morning. Pune engineers can have the rotation ready for 26 October only if they start building today, which uses four engineer-days. About half the store-days in the window run on the new fee, and customers in one catchment may see ₹35 one evening and ₹25 the next.

Option C: hold out six stores. Two stores each in Bengaluru, Hyderabad and Pune, chosen from the eleven with separate rider pools, stay on flat ₹25 until 15 November while 32 stores move to the new schedule on 26 October. Eight weeks of earlier orders from every store give the comparison its baseline. In all, 52,200 orders in three weeks run outside the new schedule. Exhibit 3 sets the three side by side.

7. Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what does Chaman Basket most need to learn from the schedule, and which of its numbers could move between 26 October and 15 November for reasons other than the fee?
  2. For each option in Exhibit 3, what stands in for "what would have happened anyway", and what would have to be true of the stores, days or customers for that stand-in to be fair?
  3. Write the decision rule for the option you favour: the primary measure, the guardrails, and the result that would stop the schedule before 16 November.
  4. Kartar Slathia argues that delay is the largest cost on the page. What would you say to him on Friday's call, and which option do you take to the chief executive?

8. A note for the learner

This case belongs to the family of decisions where the usual randomised test is unavailable or misleading, and the product manager must still say something honest about cause. The lens asks the manager to name the comparison, and the rule for reading it, before launch rather than after.

One defensible path is Option C. Kamaljit would hold out six stores from the eleven with separate rider pools, chosen before launch, and fix the decision rule on Friday: one primary measure, a ceiling on lost orders, and a stop condition on on-time delivery that applies at all 38 stores. She would use Kashish's interviews as a qualitative check beside the numbers. The reasoning is that it keeps the 26 October date Kartar needs, as Option B does, and unlike B shows each catchment a single fee all day, which meets Kashish's concern, while leaving her a comparison she can explain to a board without apologising for the calendar.

When You Can't A/B Test

Randomisation is a privilege, not a right. This is what honest causal work looks like when the privilege is withdrawn — and where competent practitioners still disagree about how much such work is worth.

Section 1Two rooms, two impossible tests

On 14 August 2026, in Bengaluru, Anirudh Sundaram had a slide he did not believe. Sundaram was chief product officer at Kshanik Health Systems, whose clinical software ran in 23 hospital groups — 146 hospitals, some 9,200 suspected-sepsis episodes a year through its early-warning module. The slide said the module reduces sepsis mortality by a fifth. Baseline mortality was 18.0%; a fifth was 3.6 percentage points. His head of clinical evidence, Dr Farida Qureshi, had told him no design available within eighteen months could distinguish 3.6 points from 1.0, and that the honest expectation was nearer 1.5. The obvious experiment — randomise which patients generate an alert — was not a design problem but an ethics problem: no review board would approve withholding a safety alert from a clinician able to act on it. Kshanik's CDSCO submission rested on a benefit claim it had not earned.

On 3 September, Meera Raghunathan sat in the Indore office of Lamha Foods, which sold namkeen through 340 distributors into some 210,000 general-trade outlets, with a decision of another shape: move its largest line from ₹10 to ₹12 with 22% more grammage — a lumpy change, since the Legal Metrology rules require declared quantity to be a permitted, printed value. The line carried ₹86 crore of annualised revenue, and against Haldiram's and Balaji on the same shelf a wrong move would surface four months later as a distributor refusing to lift stock. Raghunathan had no assignment mechanism at all: Lamha did not know its consumers, could not show two shoppers at one counter two prices, and the smallest unit it could treat was a distributor territory, between which stock moved whenever the margin justified it.

These are the same problem in different costumes: a decision worth crores, abundant data, and no way to make the data answer the question by randomising the thing they wanted to ship. What remains is a discipline — start with the estimand, diagnose which assumption broke, buy back what design can buy, state the residue honestly, decide anyway.

Section 2The idea, and the four camps that disagree about it

For each unit i there exist two potential outcomes: Yi(1) if treated, Yi(0) if not. One is observed; the causal effect is their difference; the enterprise is the construction of the unobserved half. Randomisation constructs it by making groups exchangeable in expectation, a guarantee resting on what Rubin named SUTVA: no interference, one unit's assignment does not alter another's outcome, and consistency, that "treatment" denotes one well-defined thing. "When you can't A/B test" names the repertoire — before/after with negative controls, switchbacks, cluster and geo holdouts, stepped wedges, difference-in-differences, synthetic control, qualitative designs — used when one of five obstructions removes user-level randomisation. Interference: treatment leaks through a shared pool, market or social graph. No assignment mechanism: nothing in the delivery path differentiates units, as with a shelf price. Insufficient units: too few independent units for power. Ethics or regulation: withholding is impermissible. Irreversibility: the change is one-shot, so precision is worth less than it looks. Confusing the five is the costliest error in the field, because the diagnosis selects the remedy.

The history is older than software. Neyman set out potential outcomes in 1923, Fisher formalised randomisation in 1935, Campbell and Stanley's 1963 monograph supplied the vocabulary of threats to validity. Then came the formative humiliation: LaLonde in 1986 took a randomised job-training experiment, discarded the control group, and showed that leading econometric methods applied to the remainder missed the benchmark badly and unpredictably. Dehejia and Wahba replied in 1999 that better matching recovered it; the argument has never closed. Abadie, Diamond and Hainmueller introduced synthetic control with placebo inference for a sample of one, Hussey and Hughes formalised the stepped wedge in 2007, and Gordon and colleagues in 2019 again found observational advertising-lift estimates diverging substantially from randomised benchmarks on identical data.

Four camps survive, and an expert can say what each will and will not sign. Randomisation-first signs an unrandomised estimate is a well-informed prior and should be labelled one, and refuses a placebo rank is a p-value in the sense a t-test is. Identification-first signs a pre-registered design with pre-trend tests, negative controls and placebo inference carries real decision weight, and refuses before/after with guardrails is causal evidence; it demands, for every assumption, the test that would have failed had it been violated. Decision-theoretic holds that the decision, not the estimate, is the object: it signs act when posterior expected value net of the option value of waiting clears the bar and refuses 0.05 should gate a rollout. Mechanism-first signs process tracing can rule causal stories in and out and refuses qualitative evidence can size an effect. Friction between that camp and the other three is the most reliable source of conflict in a product review.

Figure 1. The diagnosis selects the design. Reading down the left column is a triage, not a preference ordering: each obstruction has a family of answers, and each answer buys the missing counterfactual at a different price — the designs near the top pay in variance, those near the bottom pay in untestable assumption.

Section 3Mechanics: what expert practice actually consists of

Step zero: write the estimand as one sentence containing unit, contrast, outcome, population and horizon. "Does the alert help?" is not an estimand. "The average effect, among adult inpatients with a qualifying alert in Kshanik's 23 groups, of enabling the module versus standard order-set practice, on minutes from alert to first antibiotic, over six months" is. The competent practitioner picks a design; the expert runs a sequence whose first three steps precede one. Most switchback-versus-geo arguments dissolve once someone writes the sentence.

Step one: audit the interference — map its channel, range and decay rather than assert it. At Lamha the channel was trade margin, the range one or two districts along trucking corridors. At Kshanik it was clinician learning — a physician who saw good alerts on ward A changed her ordering on ward B — so patient-level randomisation would have been contaminated even had it been ethical.

Step two: compute the minimum detectable effect before choosing anything. Most alternatives die here. Cluster assignment solves interference but imposes a design effect, DEFF = 1 + (m − 1)ρ, for m observations per cluster and intra-cluster correlation ρ. Qureshi's inputs — m = 400 episodes per group per year, ρ = 0.02 — sound modest and are devastating.

Table 1. Kshanik Health Systems: what 9,200 episodes are actually worth under three designs, at 80% power and 5% two-sided significance.

Worked: DEFF = 1 + 399 × 0.02 = 8.98; effective n = 9,200/8.98 = 1,024, or 512 per arm; SE = √(2 × 0.18 × 0.82/512) = 0.024; MDE = 2.80 × 0.024 = 6.7 pp. On the antibiotic endpoint DEFF = 4.99, effective n = 1,844, SE = 4.43 min, MDE = 12.4 min.

The table holds the move that separates experts from competent practitioners, and it is not a design move. Faced with an underpowered endpoint the competent response is a cleverer design; the expert response is to change the estimand. Kshanik could not measure mortality but could measure minutes to first antibiotic — lower intra-cluster correlation, more observations, a documented link to survival. The price is a surrogacy assumption, stated formally by Prentice in 1989: the proximal endpoint must lie on the causal path and carry enough of the total effect that acting on it does not mislead.

Step three: where randomisation is impossible rather than awkward, construct the counterfactual and then attack it. Difference-in-differences assumes parallel movement absent treatment, and its falsification test is an event-study plot of pre-period leads. Synthetic control weights untreated donors to reproduce the treated unit's pre-period path, then replaces inference with a permutation: run the same procedure on every donor as though treated, and rank the treated unit's post-to-pre fit ratio in that placebo distribution. With 34 donors, first place gives p ≈ 0.029, fifth place 0.143.

Step four: build falsification into the readout in advance. A negative-control outcome is a metric the treatment could not plausibly move but every rival explanation would: if festival demand drives Lamha's numbers, it shows in the unchanged ₹20 pack in the same stores. A guardrail the treatment can move monitors harm, not confounding. Step five: quantify how wrong a confounder could make you. The E-value of VanderWeele and Ding asks how strongly an unmeasured factor must associate with both treatment and outcome to explain a result away. For a risk ratio of 0.86, invert to 1.163: E = 1.163 + √(1.163 × 0.163) = 1.60. The question becomes whether anyone can name a factor with a 1.6-fold association on both sides.

Step six: circulate the decision rule, and the value-of-information arithmetic justifying the study at all. Lamha's price move, if right, was worth about ₹9 crore of incremental annual contribution; if wrong, it risked ₹14 crore of volume decline; Raghunathan's prior put 65% on the favourable case. A thirteen-week geo test costing ₹40 lakh might move that to 85%, shifting some ₹2.4 crore of expected regret across the decision boundary — comfortably clearing its cost. Had her prior been 92%, the expert answer would have been to ship and buy reversibility instead.

Section 4The conditions, stated so they can be checked

Each design is valid conditional on claims that can be written down and tested. One: the unit of assignment contains the interference. Trace the path from one unit's treatment to another's outcome and measure along it: Kshanik passes at group level and fails at patient level, and Lamha appeared to pass at district level and did not. Two: the MDE is below the smallest effect worth acting on. Fifteen minutes of arithmetic, before launch. Kshanik fails on mortality and passes on time-to-antibiotic; Lamha's geo design had an MDE near 3.4% against a hoped-for 4%, and a design that can only just see the effect it expects usually returns an ambiguous readout. Three: a credible counterfactual exists whose pre-period fit is materially better than the effect sought. A synthetic control fitting to 2.2% of baseline can speak to a 4% effect, not a 1.5% one; Kshanik has no analogue, which is why it must randomise rollout order instead. Four: the decision is repeatable and the change reversible. Where it is, precision is worth paying for; where it is not, the money belongs in optionality — Lamha's printed packaging made the move sticky, Kshanik's module could be switched off in an afternoon.

Three situations make the repertoire misleading rather than merely weak. First, when it licenses abandoning a feasible randomisation — "we can't A/B test this" is often a scheduling admission in statistical clothing. Second, when a quasi-experimental estimate arrives with tight intervals and is granted experimental standing; the interval describes sampling variation and is silent about the assumption that generated the counterfactual. Third, when the alternative's assumptions are less checkable than the confounding it was adopted to fix.

Section 5Hard edges: platforms, regulation, hardware, AI and the organisational seam

Multi-product firms hit an estimand problem disguised as a design problem: a geo test of a new tier measures the net effect including cannibalisation, while the team that built it wants the gross number. Two-sided marketplaces suffer interference on both sides, and switchbacks handle only its temporally shared component: if a change teaches sellers something persistent, carryover does not reset at a block boundary and estimates are biased toward zero, the tell being an effect that grows as blocks lengthen.

Regulated settings substitute clinical equipoise: a trial is permissible only while genuine uncertainty remains, which is why stepped wedges became standard in health services research. Everyone receives the intervention; only the order is randomised. Kshanik's route to a defensible claim ran through a wedge registered with the Clinical Trials Registry – India; RBI sandbox cohorts are the same structure in financial clothing. Hardware plus software cuts both ways: manufacturing lots create natural experiments, since a component change from a serial range is nearly random with respect to the user, while staged over-the-air updates create the opposite, because early updaters select themselves.

AI-native products break the frame further, because the treatment is non-stationary: a model retrained on data generated under its own deployment creates a loop in which the control group's behaviour is shaped by the treatment's existence. Offline evaluation is the substitute, and it measures performance on the eval set — which, when drawn from logged interactions, inherits what users chose to ask an already-deployed system. That is the AI-era external-validity problem, and the mechanism behind the failure in Section 8.

At the organisational seam, practice diverges from what companies say publicly. Finance computes incrementality on a fiscal calendar, marketing runs media-mix models on the same rupee, product runs geo tests, and the three never agree. Firms that handle this well do not reconcile them into one figure: they assign each number the decisions it may inform, and build infrastructure rather than heroics — a permanent global holdout, a standing calendar of pre-matched market pairs, a library of past effect sizes serving as the prior for the next decision.

Section 6Eight distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The estimand, not the design, is usually what is broken. The tell is two capable people arguing switchback versus geo before anyone has written a sentence naming unit, contrast, outcome and horizon. The obvious reading, that this is a methods dispute, is wrong: they are estimating different quantities, and each is right about their own.

Interference has direction, range and decay, all measurable. The tell is "there's spillover" offered without a number. Spillover does not invalidate a design; it is a quantity. Rings of increasing distance from treated units show where it dies out, and that boundary sets the assignment unit — which is also why experts quote effective n, not the nominal count.

A good pre-period fit is necessary and nowhere near sufficient. The tell is a synthetic control with more donors than pre-periods and a near-perfect fit. The obvious reading is that the model captured the data-generating process; the correct one is that it had freedom enough to fit noise. Hold out the last pre-periods, fit on the rest, check the forecast.

A guardrail the treatment could move is not a control for confounding. The tell is a team naming revenue or retention as its guardrail. Those are harm monitors. A negative control must be something the treatment cannot touch but every rival explanation would move, and finding one is often the hardest creative act in the design.

Surrogates import an assumption that is checkable in retrospect. The tell is a readout where the proximal metric moved handsomely, the distal one did not, and the deck leads with the proximal. That the distal measure was underpowered is often true and never sufficient; state the assumption when choosing the endpoint, and schedule the check.

Researcher degrees of freedom are larger here than in A/B tests, so pre-registration matters more, not less. The tell is an analysis specification whose file timestamp postdates the intervention. Donor pool, window, seasonality adjustment and outlier rule multiply into hundreds of defensible analyses; freeze the specification against pre-period data.

"We cannot randomise" usually means "we cannot randomise the thing we want to ship." The tell is a team that has considered exactly one unit of randomisation. There is nearly always a randomisable neighbour — rollout order, timing, which accounts a success motion reaches first — answering a slightly different but decision-relevant question cleanly.

Reversibility, not sample size, should set the evidence bar. The tell is a process demanding identical rigour for a change that can be switched off in ten minutes and one that commits printed packaging for two quarters. Consistency looks like fairness; evidence is an investment whose return depends on the cost of being wrong.

Section 7How the problem changes shape across product types and stages

In consumer software units are abundant, so the binding obstruction is rarely power but interference or ethics. In B2B and enterprise it is power and heterogeneity: twenty-three accounts is a panel, not a sample, and the instinct should be within-account designs over long horizons plus matched-pair rollouts. Platforms and marketplaces add strategic adaptation — participants who detect a design respond to it, which makes long switchbacks self-defeating where sellers talk. Hardware and physical goods add measurement lag in months and irreversibility through tooling, with the compensating gift of natural experiments in lots and geography. AI products invert the usual scarcity: data is abundant and the treatment unstable, so the work migrates into evaluation design.

Stage matters in three ways. At seed stage no design rescues forty users and the honest work is qualitative. At growth stage the decisive move is infrastructure cheap to start and expensive to retrofit — a global holdout begun at 200,000 users costs almost nothing and cannot credibly be introduced at twenty million. At scale the unit of analysis shifts from the study to the portfolio. What does not change is the discipline: the estimand sentence, the MDE computed before launch, the pre-registered rule and the negative control are identical in a fifteen-person startup and a listed company. The claim that a startup is too small for them is a claim to be allowed to fool itself faster.

Section 8Three cases with the arithmetic shown

Kshanik: the design that worked by changing the question

Qureshi's protocol randomised the 23 groups into six sequences switching the module on at two-month intervals across fourteen months, registered before the first switch. The primary endpoint was minutes from alert to first antibiotic; mortality was a pre-specified secondary, monitored and explicitly not claimed. At the twelve-month interim, mean time to antibiotic was 186 minutes in untreated cluster-periods and 168 in treated ones — 18 minutes against an MDE of 12.4. Mortality moved from 18.0% to 15.5%, a risk ratio of 0.86 with an interval spanning no effect. Qureshi computed the E-value at 1.60 and wrote the sentence Sundaram later used with a hospital buyer: the mortality signal is directionally favourable, is not established by this study, and would be explained away by any unmeasured factor with a 1.6-fold association on both sides — secular improvement in sepsis protocols being one candidate.

Figure 2. The stepped wedge dissolves the ethical objection without abandoning randomisation: no group is denied the alert, and the randomised quantity is the month in which each group receives it. Each group contributes both untreated and treated periods, so comparisons run within clusters as well as between them — which is why the design effect in Table 1 falls from 8.98 to roughly 2.6.

Lamha: the design that failed, and what recovery looked like

Raghunathan's first wave treated six districts against a synthetic control of 34 donors. The fit was excellent and the separation after week zero visible to the naked eye, as Figure 3 shows; the placebo test was not. A ratio of 1.81 ranked fifth of 35 — a placebo p of 0.143 against a pre-registered rule requiring the top two. The instinct in the room was to extend the window until the result crossed. She asked instead the question that saved the programme: what would have to be true for a control district to have received the treatment? Secondary sales data answered within a day. Three donor districts adjacent to treated ones were billing volumes of the new stock-keeping unit, traders selling across the boundary at the margin the new pack afforded. The control had been partly treated, which attenuates the estimate and, because those donors carried heavy weights, corrupted the counterfactual too.

Figure 3. The synthetic control tracks the treated districts closely for a year before the price change — pre-period RMSPE of ₹3.1 lakh against a base of ₹142 lakh, or 2.2% — and then separates by roughly ₹5.6 lakh a week. The visual is persuasive and, on its own, proves nothing: the placebo distribution in Table 2 is what decides whether a gap of that size is unusual.

Recovery took two forms, neither a rescue of the original analysis. First, honesty: wave one was reported as uninformative rather than null, a distinction Raghunathan defended twice against a sales director who preferred the second reading. Second, a redesign moving assignment to the distributor territory — the boundary at which stock allocation was actually controlled — with a one-district buffer excluded from both arms, run for 26 weeks. Wave two gave a gap of ₹4.1 lakh a week and a placebo p of 0.069, which clears no conventional threshold; the decision rested instead on the value-of-information arithmetic of Section 3.

Waqtnama Labs: when the offline evaluation was the experiment

Waqtnama Labs sold an AI assistant to support operations across four contact centres staffing some 1,900 agents. Its offline evaluation was serious by industry standards: 1,200 logged tickets, expert-graded, the suggestion accepted unmodified 61% of the time, a simulation projecting an 11% cut in handle time. Online, two obstructions arrived together: agents shared a queue, so a faster treated agent changed what untreated agents received, and agents sat together and talked, so the assistant's phrasings reached the control group within a fortnight. A site-level design — two centres treated, two held back — was rejected because an n of two per arm makes any outcome consistent with any conclusion. What ran instead was a switchback at site-shift level, the first thirty minutes of each shift discarded as burn-in and a negative control tracked throughout: wrap-up time on categories the assistant did not cover.

Handle time fell 4.2%, not 11%. Decomposed by complexity the picture was worse and more useful: simple tickets improved 9.1%, complex tickets deteriorated 2.8%, because the assistant produced confident wrong suggestions that agents spent time unwinding. The evaluation missed this for a structural reason: the 1,200 tickets were sampled from historical volume, dominated by simple tickets, so the eval set encoded exactly the distribution the deployment was about to change. The negative control did not move, which let the team attribute the effect to the assistant rather than to a coincident staffing change.

Section 9Failure modes, their early warnings, and the cost of late detection

Contaminated control. Early warning: the control group's metric drifts in proportion to nearby treatment intensity. Diagnostic: what would have to be true for a control unit to receive the treatment, and can operational data show it? Cost of catching it late: an attenuated estimate and under-investment in something that worked — Lamha's near miss, caught at week 13 for one redesign rather than at month nine for a shelved line.

Power theatre. Early warning: no MDE was computed and nobody can say what the design could detect. Diagnostic: what is the smallest effect this can see, and is it below the smallest effect we would act on? Cost of catching it late: a quarter of calendar time, plus the credibility of the next four studies the team proposes.

Specification drift. Early warning: donor pool, window or outlier rule changed after the post-period was pulled. Diagnostic: what is the analysis file's timestamp relative to the intervention date? Cost of catching it late: a decision built on the most flattering of two hundred defensible analyses.

Surrogate substitution. Early warning: the headline metric is not the one in the plan. Diagnostic: when did the primary endpoint change, and who approved it? Cost of catching it late: a claim that cannot survive the first buyer who asks about the distal outcome. A fifth mode, holdout decay, works the same way — a holdout whose composition drifts through exceptions and migrations yields years of incrementality numbers that must later be withdrawn.

Section 10Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Whether quasi-experimental estimates deserve decision weight at all. The sceptical position rests on the strongest evidence in the field: LaLonde in 1986 and Gordon and colleagues in 2019 both took settings where an experimental benchmark existed, applied the best observational methods to the same data, and found divergences large enough to reverse decisions — in the advertising case, persisting after rich covariate adjustment. The proponents' reply is equally strong: the alternative to a placebo-tested synthetic control is not an experiment, because none is available; it is an executive's intuition, which carries no error bars. For the sceptics to be wrong, confounding in product settings must be milder than in advertising selection, where the system optimises for the outcome measured. For the proponents to be wrong, it must not be — and nobody has settled that empirically.

Whether permanent global holdouts earn their cost. Proponents argue that without one a company cannot separate its cumulative product work from market drift, and that a one-percent revenue tax is trivial against detecting years of effort producing nothing. Opponents argue it measures an aggregate nobody can act on, degrades through migration and exception handling, and creates a second-class experience that is ethically awkward and, under India's DPDP framework, awkward to explain. That both positions have adherents at serious companies is evidence the answer turns on facts about the firm rather than a principle.

Whether qualitative evidence can carry a ship decision. The mechanism-first argument is that with twenty-three accounts, twelve interviews using disconfirming-case selection support more reliable inference than a noisy estimate. The reply is that interview evidence has no defence against the interviewer's hypothesis, and that "directional, not sized" collapses under commercial pressure into an invented number. The usual compromise — qualitative to choose what to build, quantitative to decide whether to scale — is a truce.

Whether an offline evaluation suite counts as an experiment for AI systems. One camp holds that for non-stationary model changes evals are the only feasible control, and that treating them as second-class leads to shipping on vibes. The other holds that evals measure the eval set, that interference and behavioural adaptation are precisely what they cannot see, and that Waqtnama's 11%-versus-4.2% gap is the standard result rather than an unlucky one. This is currently the most consequential unsettled question in the area.

Section 11What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this picks designs from a menu; someone who has internalised it spends most of the effort before any design is named. They write the estimand first and notice how often the argument dissolves. They compute the minimum detectable effect in the first meeting, out loud, and will say that no available design can answer the question as posed — then propose one that can. They treat interference as a measurable quantity, never conflate a harm guardrail with a negative control, and put the assumption their estimate rests on, and the observation that would falsify it, in the deck rather than the appendix. They size the evidence investment against reversibility, which sometimes means refusing a study they could easily justify. And when a result is uninformative they say uninformative rather than null.

Section 12What the two decided

Sundaram killed the slide. Kshanik's claim became "reduces median time to first antibiotic by 18 minutes in a randomised stepped-wedge study across 23 hospital groups," with mortality reported as a monitored secondary and the E-value in the evidence pack. Two prospects who had responded to the mortality framing went quiet; three others, including the group with the most rigorous clinical procurement in the country, moved forward precisely because the claim was defensible. In a regulated market, he argued, the durable asset is the claim that survives scrutiny.

Raghunathan rolled the ₹12 pack out across the western zone after wave two, on a placebo p of 0.069 that would fail any conventional test. Her written rationale said so, then gave the value-of-information argument: the evidence had moved her probability far enough that waiting cost more in foregone contribution than another quarter of measurement could return. She also committed Lamha to something structural: the next wave's territories would receive the change in randomised order — a randomisation of timing the organisation had always had available and never used.

For discussion.

1. Sundaram traded the mortality claim for a defensible one and lost two prospects. Under what commercial conditions is that trade wrong — and would you make it at a company that needed both deals to make its quarter?

2. Raghunathan acted on a placebo p of 0.069 after pre-registering a stricter rule. Is that a principled application of decision theory, or the rule-bending she refused the sales director in wave one?

3. Waqtnama's evaluation was not wrong about the tickets it contained; it was wrong about the tickets that mattered. What would defensible eval-set governance look like, and who should own it?

  3. Testing in physical retail: test markets and store tests — the matched-market machinery behind Lamha's design, where buffer rings and trade arbitrage are the working problems.
  4. Experimentation with few, large customers — the enterprise case in full, where the customer's own change management is the largest source of variance.

  7. Experimentation culture — whether "uninformative" is a sayable word decides whether any of the above survives a quarterly review.
  8. Qual + quant feedback loop — the mechanism-first camp's methods done properly, which makes a small-n judgement defensible rather than anecdotal.
